name: The Beer–Lambert Law
statement: A sample absorbs light in proportion to its concentration and thickness.
statementAccent: in proportion to its concentration and thickness
meaning: The absorbance of a solution rises in direct proportion to how much absorbing substance it contains and how far the light travels through it. Double either the concentration or the path length and you double the absorbance, while the transmitted light falls off exponentially.
mechanism: Each successive thin layer of the sample absorbs the same fraction of the light reaching it, which makes transmitted intensity decay exponentially with depth. Taking the logarithm of the ratio of incident to transmitted light linearises this into absorbance, equal to the molar absorptivity times concentration times path length. The molar absorptivity measures how strongly a species absorbs at a given wavelength.

examples.text: Measuring a solution's absorbance to determine an unknown concentration — from a dye to bilirubin in blood plasma — is the core analytical use of the law.
A finger clip reads blood oxygen from the different light absorption of oxygenated and deoxygenated haemoglobin, an everyday medical application of the principle.
Correcting for the absorption of sunlight or starlight through the atmosphere uses the same exponential law — essentially Bouguer's original context.

variants.name: Absorbance and transmittance
variants.text: The paired quantities: transmittance is the fraction of light that gets through, and absorbance is the negative logarithm of it, which is what makes concentration and path length add linearly.

variants.name: Optical depth
variants.text: The natural-logarithm analogue used in atmospheric physics and astronomy to describe how much a medium attenuates radiation passing through it.

whyItMatters: It is the foundation of quantitative absorption spectroscopy, the reason a spectrophotometer can turn a colour into a concentration, and it reaches from chemical assays to medical sensors to atmospheric science. It is one of the most-used working relationships in analytical chemistry.

working.text: with a known molar absorptivity and path length, read concentration directly off measured absorbance.
keep concentrations dilute, roughly below a hundredth molar, and absorbance modest, where the linear relationship holds.
measure at a single well-defined wavelength, since a broad band of wavelengths breaks the law's single-wavelength assumption.

limits: The linear relationship holds only in dilute, ideal conditions. Above roughly a hundredth molar, absorbing particles stop behaving independently and interactions alter the absorptivity, and the medium's refractive index — on which absorptivity depends — itself shifts with concentration. Instrumental effects also cause deviations: non-monochromatic light, stray light, scattering by turbid samples, and fluorescence all break the assumptions. It is an empirical limiting law, accurate for dilute non-scattering samples and systematically off outside that regime.
misreadings: It is not linear at all concentrations — above about a hundredth molar it bends as particle interactions and refractive-index changes intrude. Its popular two-name form also under-credits Pierre Bouguer, who published the path-length dependence in 1729, before Lambert, who cited him.
origin: A composite law: Pierre Bouguer published the path-length dependence in 1729, Johann Heinrich Lambert gave it rigorous form in 1760 while crediting Bouguer, and August Beer added the concentration dependence in 1852 — hence the fuller name Beer–Lambert–Bouguer law.
namedAfter: August Beer and Johann Heinrich Lambert
